analysis.one_liner: Apollo Hospitals runs a network of hospitals across India, plus pharmacy distribution, diagnostic clinics (AHLL) and a digital health platform (Apollo 24|7) that is being prepared for a separate stock-market listing.
analysis.whats_happening: Q2 FY27 results are due at a board meeting on 4 November 2026, with the earnings call on 5 November - under two weeks away. In the run-up, the stock has fallen about 16% from its 23 September 2026 peak, coinciding with the Supreme Court raising concerns about hospital drug markups (late September) and a government panel's proposal to cap room rents (August 2026); a 30% margin cap on non-scheduled oncology drugs takes effect 9 November 2026. The last reported quarter, Q1 FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026), showed revenue up roughly 20% year-on-year with margins expanding.
analysis.plain_terms: Apollo is a premium, fast-growing hospital chain, but the stock is priced for that growth to continue - at roughly 52 times earnings, there isn't much room for disappointment. The tension right now is regulatory: lawmakers and courts are circling hospital pricing on drugs and room rents just as Apollo heads into results. Its digital health arm (Apollo 24|7) is finally approaching break-even after years of losses, which is a genuine positive. A separate business, the pharmacy and digital unit, is being carved out into its own listed company, so the consolidated numbers you see today won't look the same in a year or two.
analysis.quarters: Q1 FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026): consolidated revenue of roughly ₹7,043-7,044 crore, up 20-21% YoY and 7% QoQ; EBITDA of ₹1,092 crore, up 28% YoY, with margin expanding to 15.5% from 14.6% a year earlier. Reported PAT is inconsistent across sources (around ₹581 crore per the company's release versus ₹610 crore cited elsewhere) - not verified precisely, check the exact exchange filing. Within this, Healthcare Services (hospitals) revenue was ₹3,567 crore (+22% YoY) with a 24.2% EBITDA margin; occupancy ran around 70% and inpatient discharges rose 13% while average revenue per inpatient rose 8% - so growth came from both more patients and higher realisation, not one or the other. Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution plus Apollo 24|7) posted revenue of ₹2,977 crore (+20% YoY), with the digital-health cash loss narrowing to just ₹10 crore. AHLL (diagnostics/clinics) revenue was ₹499.5 crore (+15% YoY). Management raised its FY27 hospital-revenue growth guidance to around 20%.
analysis.performance_read: The stock is down 16.2% from its 23 September 2026 peak of ₹9,069 to the current ₹7,596, inside a 52-week range of ₹6,776.6-9,069. Over 1 year it is down 4.44%, but that is still better than the Nifty (-13.2%) and far better than peer Max Healthcare (-32.54%) - a relative outperformance despite the absolute dip. Over 3 years the stock is up 57.5%, ahead of both the Nifty (17.52%) and the peer (43.97%). But over 5 years, Apollo's 84.91% gain trails Max Healthcare's 145.75% by a wide margin, even as it beats the Nifty's 23.98% - so within the hospital space specifically, this peer has been the stronger long-term performer. There is no completed demerger or split distorting this price history (the 2:1 split dates back to 2010); the recent pullback lines up with regulatory headlines, not a corporate action.
analysis.valuation_read: At a P/E of roughly 52x and P/B of about 11.5x, the stock is expensive on conventional screens. Why it is priced this way: a high reported ROE (~21.2%) and ROCE (~17.4%), a premium hospital brand with continuing double-digit volume growth, and the market crediting it with eventual payoff from new bed capacity (census beds planned to rise from 9,857 toward ~14,100 by FY31) and a soon-to-be-profitable digital arm. Whether it is actually cheap: no - it is priced for roughly 20% revenue growth to continue and for the capacity expansion and digital breakeven to go to plan; any regulatory cap on drug or room pricing would bite directly into that premium.
analysis.growth_read: Growth looks genuinely volume-led as well as margin-led: inpatient discharges rose 13% YoY while average revenue per inpatient rose 8%, and the company-wide EBITDA margin still expanded from 14.6% to 15.5% alongside that volume growth. This combination - more patients and better per-patient economics at the same time - is a more durable growth story than margin expansion on flat volumes would be.
analysis.health_read: Debt/equity of about 0.90 alongside ROCE of ~17.4% and ROE of ~21.2% suggests profits are converting reasonably into returns, though exact free cash flow conversion was not independently verified here - check on Screener. Notably, the deleveraging event in 2026 was at the promoter level, not the company's: the promoter group sold a 1.3% stake for ₹1,489 crore specifically to cut personal pledge, taking promoter pledge down from 13.1% to about 2.49%. The company's balance sheet itself does not appear to be the main risk; the more live concern is business/regulatory risk - pricing caps on drugs and room rents - rather than financial risk.
analysis.ownership_read: Promoters hold about 28.02% of the company, with pledge sharply reduced from 13.1% to roughly 2.49% in 2026 after MD Suneeta Reddy and the promoter group sold a 1.3% stake to pay down promoter-level debt - a clear deleveraging signal rather than a stress sale of the underlying business. FIIs hold around 41-43%, mutual funds about 17.33% (rising from the prior quarter), and LIC holds 2.17% directly. No widely known marquee value investor appears on the register in the sources checked here - that absence is worth noting plainly rather than assuming one exists.
strengths: EBITDA margin expanded from 14.6% to 15.5% YoY in Q1 FY27 even as revenue grew ~20%
Apollo 24|7's digital-health cash loss narrowed to just ₹10 crore in Q1 FY27, nearing breakeven after years of losses
Promoter pledge cut from 13.1% to ~2.49% in 2026, removing a leverage-driven overhang
Inpatient discharges up 13% YoY alongside 8% higher revenue per inpatient - growth from both volume and pricing, not one alone
watchpoints: Regulatory pressure building: a 30% margin cap on non-scheduled oncology drugs takes effect 9 November 2026, alongside a room-rent-cap proposal (Aug 2026) and Supreme Court scrutiny of hospital markups (late Sept 2026) - all of which coincided with the recent 16% stock pullback
Valuation is rich at roughly 52x P/E and 11.5x P/B, leaving little room for a growth or margin miss
Q1 FY27 PAT is reported inconsistently across sources (around ₹581 crore vs ₹610 crore) - the exact figure needs direct verification from the exchange filing before quoting
Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution and digital health) is slated for a separate listing around Q4 FY27, which will eventually break comparability in consolidated results
analysis.one_thing: The Q2 FY27 results due at the 4 November 2026 board meeting - specifically whether EBITDA margin keeps expanding and whether management holds its ~20% growth guidance in light of the new drug-pricing caps - will show whether the regulatory headlines are denting actual economics or just sentiment.
analysis.data_notes: Q1 FY27 revenue and EBITDA figures were cross-checked across multiple independent sources and agreed closely. PAT for both Q1 FY27 and Q4 FY26 varied across sources (e.g. ₹581cr vs ₹610cr; ₹529cr/₹541cr/₹551cr) and could not be reconciled - treat as approximate. DII shareholding percentage showed an unreconciled discrepancy (1.77% vs 22.07%) across sources - not verified, check on Screener. P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE and D/E were pulled from secondary/cached search snippets rather than a live Screener fetch and should be reconfirmed before publication; they move daily and the stock traded in a ₹7,600-7,871 range through October 2026.
